vocabulary.definition: The structure or plan of a piece of music.

study.title: Mapping Music
study.question: How is music organized into sections?
study.passage:
Forms guide (written for this lesson):
Binary (AB): two contrasting sections, often each repeated (AABB); common in Baroque dances.
Ternary (ABA): A, contrasting B, then A returns. "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" is a simple ABA.
Rondo (ABACA): A keeps returning. Beethoven's "Für Elise" (written around 1810) is a well-known rondo.
Verse-chorus form: Intro, Verse 1, (Pre-chorus), Chorus, Verse 2, (Pre-chorus), Chorus, Bridge, Chorus, Outro.
Bridge: a contrasting section, often with new chords, before the last chorus.
Activities: 1. Listen to Twinkle and Für Elise; use letters to map each. 2. Listen to two school-appropriate pop songs; write the section and the time it starts (e.g. 0:00 Intro, 0:12 Verse 1). 3. Create a form map poster with colour-coded sections. 4. Compare: which form appears in both classical and pop music?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Für Elise is in the public domain.

study.title: Canada's Soundtrack
study.question: Who are Canada's musicians and how do they shape music?
study.passage:
Artist gallery (summary written for this lesson; dates are from public records):
Joni Mitchell: singer-songwriter born in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in 1943 and raised in Saskatchewan; known for folk albums such as Blue (1971) and open guitar tunings.
Oscar Peterson (1925–2007): jazz pianist from Montreal, famous for speed and swing; composed the "Canadiana Suite" (1964).
Gordon Lightfoot (1938–2023): folk songwriter from Orillia, Ontario; "Canadian Railroad Trilogy" (1967) tells the story of building the railway.
Leonard Cohen (1934–2016): Montreal poet-songwriter; "Hallelujah" (1984) has been covered many times.
Tanya Tagaq: Inuk singer from Nunavut who uses throat singing in experimental music; won the Polaris Music Prize in 2014 for Animism.
Jeremy Dutcher: Wolastoqiyik tenor and composer from New Brunswick; won the Polaris Prize in 2018 for an album sung in Wolastoqey, built around archival recordings of his ancestors.
Policy: The CRTC introduced Canadian content rules for radio in 1971; today commercial radio must play at least 35% Canadian popular music.
Activity: rotate through stations listening to short excerpts; record genre, instruments, features and what makes each artist distinctive.

study.title: Spotlight on a Canadian Artist
study.question: How do I present a musician so the audience understands their music?
study.passage:
Presentation guide (written for this lesson):
Choose: one Canadian musician or group from any genre or era (folk, jazz, classical, country, hip hop, rock, pop, Indigenous, francophone). Check with your teacher that the music is school-appropriate.
Research (2 lessons): use at least three reliable sources: e.g. The Canadian Encyclopedia, the artist's official website, the Juno Awards or Polaris sites, a library database or a major news outlet. Record citations as you go.
Content (4–5 minutes): 1. Background: where they're from and how they began. 2. Style: genre, instruments, voice, lyrics, form. 3. Two musical examples (30 seconds each) with what to listen for. 4. Impact: awards, influence, community or cultural importance. 5. Your opinion with reasons.
Slides: images and key words, not paragraphs.
End with a works-cited slide and take two questions.
Peer rubric: accurate content, clear musical examples, explained features using music vocabulary, confident delivery, sources cited.
